hints: Look closely at the y-axis, mass of nuclear DNA in a cell. Notice the slow rise from 2 to 4 and then the sudden vertical drop from 4 back to 2. What must happen to add DNA, then to lose half of it from one cell?

Remember that nuclear division alone would leave two nuclei inside one cell, so the total DNA mass in that cell would stay at 4. Think about which extra process is needed to return a single cell to 2.
walkthrough:
**Read what the graph is tracking**

Look at the labels carefully. The y-axis is mass of nuclear DNA in a cell, not in a nucleus. That little word, in a cell, is the key to the whole question.

We start at $2$ units, rise to $4$ units, stay there, then drop straight back to $2$ units.

**Explain the slow rise from 2 to 4**

This is DNA replication in S phase of interphase. Each chromosome is copied, so the DNA content doubles.

$$2 \text{ units} \rightarrow 4 \text{ units} = \text{DNA replication}$$

**Explain the sudden fall from 4 to 2**

This is where students often get caught. Nuclear division (mitosis) alone splits one nucleus into two, but both nuclei would still be in the same cell, so the mass per cell would stay at 4.

To get back to 2 in one cell, the cytoplasm must also divide and separate the two nuclei into two daughter cells. That is cytokinesis following nuclear division.

$$4 \text{ units} \rightarrow 2 \text{ units} = \text{nuclear division + cytokinesis}$$

**Put it all together**

The full cycle shown needs all three: DNA replication to double the DNA, nuclear division to separate it, and cytokinesis to split the cell and halve the DNA per cell. That matches option B.

options.A: Close, but incomplete. Without cytokinesis the cell would stay binucleate with mass 4, so it cannot explain the drop back to 2.
options.B: Correct. The rise shows DNA replication, and the drop from 4 to 2 in a cell shows nuclear division plus cytokinesis producing two daughter cells.
options.C: Mitosis and cytokinesis explain the drop, but they do not explain the rise from 2 to 4, which is DNA replication in interphase, not part of mitosis.
options.D: Mitosis alone explains neither the doubling in S phase nor the halving per cell, which needs cytokinesis as well.
